OpenZess Studio: A Web-Native, AI-Augmented Aerothermal CFD Platform Fusing Fractional-Step Navier--Stokes Solvers, Physics-Informed Neural Surrogates, and Bare-Metal Rust SIMD Acceleration
Debjit Bhattacharya
Dept. of Computing Technologies, School of Computing
SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Chennai, India
Project Identifier: UR2627GEN317 • debjitbhattacharya@srmist.edu.in
Roshni Rakshit
Dept. of Computing Technologies, School of Computing
SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Chennai, India
Project Identifier: UR2627GEN317 • roshnirakshit@srmist.edu.in
Abstract—Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) workflows in aerospace, automotive, and marine engineering have historically been constrained by heavy compute requirements, proprietary license expenses (≈$30,000/seat/year), and steep technical barriers imposed by command-line interfaces. In this paper, we present OpenZess Studio, an indigenous, open-source, web-native CFD and aerothermal simulation ecosystem that bridges the gap between compute-intensive numerical solvers and interactive real-time design exploration. OpenZess unifies three distinct computational engines within a single reactive framework: (i) an indigenous continuous 3D incompressible Navier--Stokes solver employing Chorin's fractional-step projection method, Boussinesq thermal buoyancy, hydrostatic pressure gradients, and an Immersed Boundary Method (IBM) for arbitrary solid geometries; (ii) an instant Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) surrogate model providing sub-50 ms steady-state flow and thermal field estimations; and (iii) a bare-metal multi-threaded Rust micro-service utilizing Rayon work-stealing concurrency and AVX-256 SIMD vector stencils to bypass Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL). Physical state variables and logarithmic residuals are streamed over full-duplex binary WebSockets to an in-browser Three.js WebGL viewport rendering 60 FPS orthogonal slicing (XY, XZ, YZ), continuous 3D ribbon streamlines, and real-time SimScale-calibrated scalar probe telemetry (Umax, Uavg, Prange, Comax). Quantitative validation against the canonical Ghia et al. (1982) lid-driven cavity benchmark confirms high physical fidelity (R2 > 0.985, NRMSE < 3.2%). Spatial discretization error analysis using Roache's Grid Convergence Index (GCI) across three grid hierarchies (213, 413, 613) demonstrates asymptotic spatial convergence with GCI23 = 1.48%. Execution benchmarks reveal that the compiled Rust SIMD stencil completes an elliptic pressure-projection cycle in 3.7 ms on a 643 grid, yielding an 11.4× acceleration over pre-factored SciPy sparse linear algebra and a 130.2× speedup over interpreted CPython. Finally, the platform provides automated two-way synchronization with official OpenFOAM case directories and legacy VTK post-processing pipelines.
Keywords—Computational Fluid Dynamics, Fractional-Step Projection, Physics-Informed Neural Networks, Rust SIMD, WebGL Three.js, OpenFOAM, Grid Convergence Index, Hydrodynamics, Immersed Boundary Method.

I. Introduction

Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) serves as an indispensable cornerstone of modern scientific and industrial engineering, dictating aerodynamic efficiency in aeronautics, thermal heat dissipation in high-density data infrastructure, and hydrodynamic optimization in naval architecture. Despite remarkable numerical advances over the past five decades, the practical deployment of CFD remains plagued by severe operational bottlenecks that inhibit rapid, iterative engineering prototyping.

A. The Traditional CFD Bottleneck

Industrial-grade simulation packages such as ANSYS Fluent, Siemens STAR-CCM+, and COMSOL Multiphysics rely on proprietary, closed-source ecosystems characterized by exorbitant commercial licensing fees, often exceeding $30,000 per user seat annually. These tools demand dedicated high-performance computing (HPC) clusters or specialized workstation hardware, rendering them largely inaccessible to academic researchers, early-stage startups, and distributed engineering teams.

Conversely, open-source finite volume suites, most notably OpenFOAM, offer peer-reviewed physical fidelity and extensive turbulence modeling libraries without licensing restrictions. However, OpenFOAM relies fundamentally on complex text-based dictionary configuration files (system/controlDict, system/fvSchemes, 0/U, 0/p), manual meshing pipelines (blockMesh, snappyHexMesh), and headless Linux command-line execution. This paradigm imposes a steep learning curve, disconnects simulation setup from real-time spatial intuition, and necessitates clumsy offline file transfers to standalone post-processors like ParaView for visualization.

B. Physics-Informed Neural Surrogates

To mitigate the computational cost of iterative PDE solutions, the scientific computing community has increasingly turned toward deep learning surrogates. Raissi et al. formulated Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), demonstrating that embedding non-linear Navier--Stokes differential operators directly into the loss function enables accurate velocity and pressure field estimation without massive labeled training corpora. Concurrently, operator learning paradigms such as Fourier Neural Operators (FNO) and DeepONets have exhibited order-of-magnitude accelerations in parametric flow inference.

Nevertheless, existing physics-informed machine learning frameworks exist predominantly as siloed research code written in PyTorch or TensorFlow. They operate offline in Jupyter notebooks, lack integrated geometric modeling capabilities, and do not provide interactive bidirectional coupling to running numerical solvers or web-native visualization environments.

C. Research Contributions

To resolve these dichotomies, we introduce OpenZess Studio (Project UR2627GEN317), an integrated browser-native aerothermal CFD platform. The core contributions of this research are:

1) Multi-Engine Compute Architecture: Coupling an indigenous 3D fractional-step Navier--Stokes finite volume solver with an instant PINN surrogate and a bare-metal multi-threaded Rust micro-service, bypassing Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) via binary WebSocket IPC.

2) High-Fidelity Physical Parity: Implementation of Boussinesq thermal buoyancy, hydrostatic pressure gradients (ρgh), high-salinity ocean seawater media (ρ = 1025 kg/m3), cavitation inception indexing (σ), and dynamic discrete surface force integrals for lift (Cl), drag (Cd), and aerodynamic downforce.

3) Interactive Parametric Solid Modeling: A continuous Immersed Boundary Method (IBM) engine supporting analytical NACA 4-digit airfoils, bluff cylinders, multi-rotor drone downwash, and custom geometry generation with real-time chord angle of attack (α) rotation.

4) Real-Time WebGL Scientific Visualization: A Three.js client delivering 60 FPS multi-axis orthogonal slicing, continuous 3D ribbon streamlines, in-situ SimScale-style statistical probes, and zero-cache deployment guarantees.

5) Automated Industrial Interoperability: Direct two-way regex synchronization with OpenFOAM case hierarchies and exportable production bundles ready for Linux cluster execution.

II. Mathematical Formulations

A. Incompressible Navier--Stokes Equations

The fluid continuum within computational domain Ω ⊂ ℝ3 is governed by continuous mass and momentum conservation under gravitational and thermal buoyancy body forces:

∇ · u = 0 (1)
∂u∂t + (u · ∇)u = −1ρ∇p + ν∇2u + g + gβ(T − Tamb) (2)

where u = (u, v, w)T denotes fluid velocity, p is kinematic pressure, ν is kinematic viscosity, ρ is fluid density, g = (0, 0, −9.81 m/s2)T is gravitational acceleration, and β = 1/Tamb is the thermal expansion coefficient.

B. Thermal Energy Transport

Thermal advection and diffusion through the moving fluid continuum are captured via the continuous energy equation:

∂T∂t + (u · ∇)T = αth ∇2T + q̇Vρ cp (3)

where αth is thermal diffusivity, cp is isobaric heat capacity, and q̇V represents volumetric heat generation.

C. Marine Hydrodynamics & Cavitation

For high-salinity seawater media (ρ = 1025.0 kg/m3, ν = 1.05 × 10−6 m2/s), hydrostatic pressure and cavitation inception index σ are evaluated as:

Δphydro = ρ g h,    σ = p∞ − pvap½ ρ U∞2 (4)

where h is submerged water depth and pvap ≈ 2338 Pa is water vapor saturation pressure at 20°C. Critical cavitation risk is flagged whenever σ ≤ 1.0.

D. Chorin's Fractional-Step Discretization

Governing equations are decoupled using Chorin's projection scheme:

Step 1 (Intermediate Predictor): Non-linear convective transport and diffusion are evaluated explicitly:

u* = un + Δt [ ν∇2un − (un · ∇)un + g + gβ(Tn − Tamb) ] (5)

Step 2 (Elliptic Pressure-Poisson): Enforcing mass incompressibility ∇ · un+1 = 0 yields:

∇2p = ρΔt ∇ · u* (6)

Step 3 (Velocity Corrector): The physical divergence-free velocity field is corrected:

un+1 = u* − Δtρ ∇p (7)

E. Immersed Boundary Solid Masking

Solid bodies are immersed via spatial masking indicator functions χ(x) ∈ {0, 1}. For analytical NACA 4-digit airfoils, thickness distributions yt are computed as:

yt = 0.6c [ 0.2969√(x/c) − 0.1260(x/c) − 0.3516(x/c)2 + 0.2843(x/c)3 − 0.1015(x/c)4 ] (8)

with coordinate rotation through angle of attack α:

x' = (x − cx)cos(α) + (y − cy)sin(α),   y' = −(x − cx)sin(α) + (y − cy)cos(α) (9)

F. Dynamic Surface Stress Integration

Dynamic lift (Cl), drag (Cd), and downforce (Fdown) are computed via discrete surface integrals of local pressure and viscous shear stress:

Ftotal = ∮∂Ωsolid [ −p n + μ(∇u + (∇u)T)n ] dA (10)
C_d = Fx½ ρ U∞2 A,   C_l = Fy½ ρ U∞2 A,   Fdown = ½ ρ U∞2 A |C_l| (11)

III. Hybrid System Architecture

To achieve real-time 60 FPS interaction without compromising physical accuracy, OpenZess Studio implements a distributed tripartite architecture:

A. Bare-Metal Rust Sidecar

To bypass Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), the inner Pressure-Poisson linear solve is compiled as an independent native binary using Rust 2024. Rayon work-stealing parallelism distributes domain sub-slices across CPU threads, while AVX-256 SIMD intrinsics process 8 single-precision values per clock cycle. The sidecar communicates over asynchronous WebSockets (port 8081) with sub-10 ms binary IPC round-trip latency.

B. Central FastAPI Gateway

The Python server orchestrates client sessions, parses OpenFOAM dimensioned scalar syntax (deltaT, nu, internalField) via regular expressions to override solver states live, and serializes case snapshots to disk storage (/api/projects) with client-side localStorage fallback. Strict ASGI anti-caching middleware ensures deterministic bundle delivery on localhost:8000.

C. Three.js WebGL Scientific Viewport

Built with Vue 3 and TypeScript, the client features a 4-tab control center (Physics & Water, Geometry & Custom Builder, Case Tree, and History & Save), rendering orthogonal dynamic cut-planes (XY, XZ, YZ) shaded across five perceptually uniform colormaps (Turbo, Coolwarm, Jet, Viridis, Inferno) and RK4 ribbon streamlines.

IV. Verification & Benchmark Results

A. Ghia et al. (1982) Cavity Validation

Numerical accuracy was benchmarked on the 2D lid-driven square cavity flow at Re = 100 with lid velocity Ulid = 1.0 m/s. As displayed in Fig. 2, extracted centerline velocity profiles u(y) at x = 0.5 and v(x) at y = 0.5 exhibit near-perfect agreement with canonical Ghia et al. (1982) experimental datasets. Statistical regression confirms high fidelity with coefficient of determination R2 = 0.9850 and normalized root-mean-square error NRMSE = 3.12%.

Fig. 2. Centerline velocity profiles u(y) at x = 0.5 (left) and v(x) at y = 0.5 (right) benchmarked against published Ghia et al. (1982) data (Re = 100), demonstrating R2 = 0.9850 and NRMSE = 3.12%.

B. Residual Convergence History

Asymptotic convergence was monitored by calculating the L2 error norm across consecutive time steps. As depicted in Fig. 3, momentum and pressure residuals exhibit stable, monotonic logarithmic decay below the stopping tolerance of 10−5 within 214 iterations, verifying numerical stability and absence of checkerboard pressure oscillations.

Fig. 3. Logarithmic asymptotic convergence history of velocity divergence and pressure residuals decaying stably below 10−5 within 214 iterations.

C. Grid Independence & Roache GCI

Spatial discretization uncertainty was assessed using three systematically refined Cartesian grids: coarse (212), medium (412), and fine (612) with refinement ratio r ≈ 2.0. Following Roache's GCI guidelines, the calculated index dropped to GCI23 = 1.48%, verifying that spatial discretization error is safely bounded.

D. PINN Surrogate Field Estimation

The integrated PINN surrogate evaluates steady-state velocity vector and scalar pressure fields via a composite loss penalizing boundary discrepancies and Navier--Stokes PDE residuals. As shown in Fig. 4, the surrogate reproduces core recirculation structures with an inference latency of just 2.68 ms and MAE = 0.54 m/s, enabling instant parametric steering prior to full solver execution.

E. Multi-Engine Latency Benchmarks

Execution latency was benchmarked on an 8-core CPU across a 64 × 64 grid (Table III). The compiled Rust SIMD stencil executes a complete projection step in 3.7 ms, delivering an 11.4× acceleration over SciPy banded CSR and a 130.2× speedup over interpreted CPython, with memory consumption held at just 24 MB.

V. Case Studies & OpenFOAM Export

A. Multi-Archetype Flow Dynamics

The platform was benchmarked across five canonical flow archetypes:

1) NACA Airfoil: Evaluated across α ∈ [−5°, +20°]. Thin-airfoil lift (Cl = 2πsinα · 0.88) accurately reproduces pre-stall lift and wake recirculation (Cl = 0.82, Cd = 0.058, L/D = 14.1 at α = 8°).

2) Formula 1 Chassis: Aerodynamic multi-element wings and underbody diffuser profiles produce ground-effect downforce (Fdown = 4.8 kN, Cl = −2.85, Cd = 0.92).

3) Multi-Rotor Drone: Twin counter-rotating rotor discs generate continuous vertical downwash (Thrust = 17.65 N, Cl = 1.20, Cd = 0.32).

4) Submarine Hull: Hydrodynamic hull with conning tower in ocean seawater exhibits low drag (Cd = 0.082) and cavitation hotspot tracking (σ = 18.42).

5) Circular Cylinder: Periodic von Kármán vortex shedding downstream with Strouhal number St = 0.20 and oscillating lift Cl = ±0.08.

B. Production OpenFOAM Case Compilation

OpenZess bridges academic exploration and industrial deployment via its automated OpenFOAM export pipeline (backend/openfoam_export.py). It synthesizes complete case directories (system/controlDict, fvSchemes, fvSolution, constant/transportProperties, 0/U, 0/p, 0/T) calibrated for official OpenFOAM Foundation solvers (simpleFoam, buoyantBoussinesqSimpleFoam), alongside legacy structured-points VTK files (.vtk) for ParaView.

VI. Conclusion & Future Work

OpenZess Studio establishes that modern web-native architectures, when coupled with bare-metal compiled stencils and physics-informed neural surrogates, can execute scientific CFD workflows in real time directly within consumer web browsers. Quantitative validation against the Ghia et al. (1982) benchmark confirms high physical fidelity (R2 > 0.985), while Roache's GCI (1.48%) verifies spatial grid independence. The compiled Rust SIMD sidecar delivers an 11.4× speedup over SciPy and 130.2× over interpreted CPython, enabling 60 FPS in-situ slice probing.

Future research will focus on deploying client-side WebGPU compute shaders for 100,000+ particle ribbons, incorporating RANS turbulence closures (k-ε, k-ω SST) within the Rust sidecar, and automating triangulated 3D STL CAD surface voxelization into OpenFOAM snappyHexMeshDict.
